t: #3681 Maximum XOR of Subsequences — Linear Basis
o: X and Y are each XORs of subsets, i.e., elements of the linear span S of nums over GF(2). Since S is closed under XOR, X ^ Y ranges exactly over S (any Z ∈ S is achieved with Y = 0, X = Z). So the answer is the classic maximum subset XOR: build a Gaussian-elimination basis of nums and greedily combine basis vectors from the highest bit down. Values ≤ 10^9 < 2^30, so 30 bit-buckets suffice.
k: Subset XORs form a GF(2) linear space; it is closed under XOR, so {X ^ Y} = the entire span.
Maximum subset XOR = greedy over a reduced linear basis from the highest bit downward.

a.i: Insert each number into the basis: reduce it against existing pivots from the high bit down; if a pivot slot is free, store it there. Then fold: res = max(res, res ^ basis[b]) for b from high to low — each step either keeps or flips bit b to 1 without disturbing higher bits.
s: basis[b] holds a vector whose highest set bit is b.
For each x: for b from 29 down, if bit b set, x ^= basis[b] if occupied, else place and break.
Fold greedily from b = 29 down to get the maximum.
a.t: O(n · 30) for basis construction plus O(30) for the greedy fold

a.i: Equivalent linear algebra with a dynamic basis list: process numbers in descending order, reducing each against all current basis vectors (taking x = min(x, x ^ b) lowers the rank whenever the top bits match), keeping nonzero remainders as new pivots. The final greedy fold is identical; this variant adapts easily to arbitrary-width integers.
s: Sort nums descending; maintain a descending-sorted basis list.
Reduce each x against every b: x = min(x, x ^ b); append x if nonzero.
Fold res = max(res, res ^ b) over the basis.
a.t: O(n log n + n·D) with D ≤ 30 reduction steps per number (plus small resort costs)

w: Prove the span-closure claim first — it reduces the two-subsequence problem to standard maximum subset XOR. Pitfalls: iterating basis bits low-to-high in the fold (breaks greediness), and assuming overlapping subsequences matter (they don't — closure makes the choice free). Follow-up: k-th smallest subset XOR (build the basis, then standard k-th enumeration), or maximum subset AND/OR.
